const std = @import("std");
const rl = @import("raylib");
const net = std.net;
const posix = std.posix;
const mem = std.mem;

/// Define your controller event indices based on the JSON mapping
const ControllerEvents = enum(i16) {
    ANALOG_LX = 0,
    ANALOG_LY = 1,
    ANALOG_RX = 2,
    ANALOG_RY = 3,
    L1 = 4,
    L2 = 5,
    R1 = 6,
    R2 = 7,
    TRIANGLE = 8,
    CROSS = 9,
    SQUARE = 10,
    CIRCLE = 11,
    UP = 12,
    DOWN = 13,
    LEFT = 14,
    RIGHT = 15,
    SELECT = 16,
    START = 17,
};

const EventPair = struct {
    index: i16,
    value: i16,
};

/// Send an entire array of EventPairs to the server.
fn sendControllerState(
    sock: posix.fd_t,
    addr: *const net.Address,
    eventPairs: []const EventPair,
) !void {
    const sockaddr = &addr.any;
    const addrlen = addr.getOsSockLen();
    const bytesToSend = mem.asBytes(eventPairs);
    const totalBytes = bytesToSend.len;

    const ret = try posix.sendto(sock, bytesToSend, 0, sockaddr, addrlen);
    std.debug.print("Sent {d} bytes\n", .{ret});

    if (ret != totalBytes) {
        std.log.warn("Warning: Not all data was sent. Expected to send {d} bytes, but sent {d}\n",
            .{ totalBytes, ret });
    }
}

/// Create a UDP socket (for sending only)
fn createUDPSocket() !posix.fd_t {
    return posix.socket(posix.AF.INET, posix.SOCK_DGRAM, 0);
}

/// Initialize controller state; one value per event.
fn initializeControllerState() [@intFromEnum(ControllerEvents.START) + 1]i16 {
    var controllerState: [@intFromEnum(ControllerEvents.START) + 1]i16 = undefined;
    @memset(controllerState[0..], 0);
    return controllerState;
}

pub fn main() anyerror!void {
    const alloc = std.heap.page_allocator;

    // Initialization parameters
    const screenWidth = 800;
    const screenHeight = 450;

    rl.initWindow(screenWidth, screenHeight, "raylib-zig example - keyboard to controller input");
    defer rl.closeWindow();

    rl.setTargetFPS(60);

    // Initialize controller state (one value per event)
    var controllerState = initializeControllerState();

    // Create a UDP socket for sending packets
    const sock = try createUDPSocket();
    defer posix.close(sock);

    while (!rl.windowShouldClose()) {
        // Update controller state based on keyboard input.
        // (For this example, we update only the four directional keys.)
        controllerState[@intFromEnum(ControllerEvents.UP)] = if (rl.isKeyDown(rl.KeyboardKey.key_up)) 1 else 0;
        controllerState[@intFromEnum(ControllerEvents.DOWN)] = if (rl.isKeyDown(rl.KeyboardKey.key_down)) 1 else 0;
        controllerState[@intFromEnum(ControllerEvents.LEFT)] = if (rl.isKeyDown(rl.KeyboardKey.key_left)) 1 else 0;
        controllerState[@intFromEnum(ControllerEvents.RIGHT)] = if (rl.isKeyDown(rl.KeyboardKey.key_right)) 1 else 0;

        // Build an array of EventPair where each pair contains the event index and its value.
        const eventCount = @intFromEnum(ControllerEvents.START) + 1;
        var eventPairs: [eventCount]EventPair = undefined;
        // Fill in all events – the index is implicit in the array order
        var i: usize = 0;
        while (i < eventCount) : (i += 1) {
            eventPairs[i] = EventPair{
                .index = @intCast(i16, i),
                .value = controllerState[i],
            };
        }

        // Create the destination address; using localhost here.
        const addr = try net.Address.parseIp4("127.0.0.1", 31415);
        try sendControllerState(sock, &addr, eventPairs[0..]);

        // Draw screen
        rl.beginDrawing();
        rl.clearBackground(rl.Color.white);
        rl.drawText("Press arrow keys to simulate controller input!", 190, 200, 20, rl.Color.lightGray);
        rl.endDrawing();
    }
}
-----------------------------------------------------------

1. On the C side, the UDP server now expects a binary packet containing an array of pairs (each pair is 4 bytes in total, two int16_t’s). The server iterates over each pair, validates that the event index is within range, writes the virtual event, and then sends a synchronization event.

2. On the Zig side, instead of sending a raw array of values, we build an array of EventPair structs such that each pair explicitly carries its event index and value. This way the information on “which event” and its “state” is self‐contained, matching the “example Zig array” format.

By making these modifications, both the server and the client agree on the same binary format for transmitting the controller state.

We can solve this problem by “merging” the existing connected components using the cheapest available new roads. The key observation is that if the city currently has several connected components (determined by the m pre‐built roads) then we only need to add k–1 roads (where k is the number of components) so that the network becomes fully connected.

Moreover, since the cost of constructing a new road between two houses is defined as the sum of the prices of the two houses, to keep the additional cost minimal we should always use the cheapest available house in each component. In fact, if we take the component that has the overall cheapest house in the city and then connect every other component to it using that cheapest house from the other component, the cost for each extra road is minimized. (This “star” strategy is well known for problems where connecting two components costs sum of representatives’ weights.)

The steps are as follows:

1. Read the input and make a union–find (Disjoint Set Union, DSU) structure for the n houses.
2. Process the m pre‐built roads to “merge” the connected components.
3. Then, for every component, determine its cheapest house (the one with the smallest price).
4. Find among these the overall cheapest house (say house X). This will be used to connect to the cheapest house from every other component.
5. For every component different from X’s component, add a road between house X and the cheapest house in that component.
6. Finally, print the number of added roads and the list of new roads.

#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;
 
// Disjoint Set Union (Union-Find)
struct DSU {
    int n;
    vector<int> parent;
    DSU(int n) : n(n), parent(n+1) {
        for (int i = 0; i <= n; i++) {
            parent[i] = i;
        }
    }
    int find(int a) {
        if (parent[a] == a) return a;
        return parent[a] = find(parent[a]);
    }
    void unite(int a, int b) {
        a = find(a);
        b = find(b);
        if (a != b)
            parent[b] = a;
    }
};
 
int main(){

    cin.tie(nullptr);
    
    int n, m;
    cin >> n >> m;
 
    vector<long long> price(n+1);
    for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++){
        cin >> price[i];
    }
 
    DSU dsu(n);
    // Process the existing roads
    for (int i = 0; i < m; i++){
        int u, v;
        cin >> u >> v;
        dsu.unite(u, v);
    }
 
    // Map each component representative to its cheapest house (price and vertex)
    unordered_map<int, pair<long long,int>> comp;
    for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++){
        int rep = dsu.find(i);
        if (comp.find(rep) == comp.end()){
            comp[rep] = { price[i], i };
        } else {
            if (price[i] < comp[rep].first)
                comp[rep] = { price[i], i };
        }
    }
 
    // If there's only one component then no new roads are needed.
    int numComponents = comp.size();
    if(numComponents == 1){
        cout << 0 << "\n";
        return 0;
    }
 
    // Identify the global minimum house among all components.
    long long globalMin = LLONG_MAX;
    int globalVertex = -1, globalRep = -1;
    for (auto &entry : comp){
        if (entry.second.first < globalMin) {
            globalMin = entry.second.first;
            globalVertex = entry.second.second;
            globalRep = entry.first;
        }
    }
 
    // Build a road from the global minimum house to the cheapest house in every other component.
    vector<pair<int,int>> addedRoads;
    for (auto &entry : comp){
        if (entry.first == globalRep) continue;
        addedRoads.push_back({globalVertex, entry.second.second});
    }
 
    cout << addedRoads.size() << "\n";
    for (auto &e : addedRoads)
        cout << e.first << " " << e.second << "\n";
 
    return 0;
}

### Approach
1. **Identify Connected Components**: Use a Disjoint Set Union (DSU) to find all connected components in the graph formed by existing roads.
2. **Track Minimum House Prices**: For each connected component, track the house with the minimum price and its index.
3. **Global Minimum Component**: Determine the component with the globally minimum house price. This component will be the central point to which all other components will be connected.

#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <unordered_set>
#include <climits>

using namespace std;

struct DSU {
    vector<int> parent;
    vector<int> rank;
    vector<int> min_a;
    vector<int> min_index;
    
    DSU(int n, vector<int>& a) {
        parent.resize(n);
        rank.resize(n, 1);
        min_a.resize(n);
        min_index.resize(n);
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            parent[i] = i;
            min_a[i] = a[i];
            min_index[i] = i;
        }
    }
    
    int find(int u) {
        if (parent[u] != u) {
            parent[u] = find(parent[u]);
        }
        return parent[u];
    }
    
    void unite(int u, int v) {
        int ru = find(u);
        int rv = find(v);
        if (ru == rv) return;
        if (rank[ru] > rank[rv]) {
            swap(ru, rv);
        }
        parent[ru] = rv;
        if (rank[ru] == rank[rv]) {
            rank[rv]++;
        }
        if (min_a[ru] < min_a[rv]) {
            min_a[rv] = min_a[ru];
            min_index[rv] = min_index[ru];
        } else if (min_a[ru] == min_a[rv]) {
            if (min_index[ru] < min_index[rv]) {
                min_index[rv] = min_index[ru];
            }
        }
    }
};

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);
    
    int n, m;
    cin >> n >> m;
    vector<int> a(n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        cin >> a[i];
    }
    
    DSU dsu(n, a);
    for (int i = 0; i < m; i++) {
        int u, v;
        cin >> u >> v;
        dsu.unite(u - 1, v - 1);
    }
    
    unordered_set<int> roots;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        roots.insert(dsu.find(i));
    }
    
    int k = roots.size();
    if (k == 1) {
        cout << "0\n";
        return 0;
    }
    
    vector<pair<int, int>> components;
    for (int r : roots) {
        components.emplace_back(dsu.min_a[r], dsu.min_index[r]);
    }
    
    int global_min_a = INT_MAX;
    int global_min_idx = -1;
    for (const auto& comp : components) {
        if (comp.first < global_min_a || (comp.first == global_min_a && comp.second < global_min_idx)) {
            global_min_a = comp.first;
            global_min_idx = comp.second;
        }
    }
    
    vector<pair<int, int>> edges;
    for (const auto& comp : components) {
        if (comp.second == global_min_idx) continue;
        edges.emplace_back(global_min_idx + 1, comp.second + 1); // Convert to 1-based
    }
    
    cout << edges.size() << '\n';
    for (const auto& edge : edges) {
        cout << edge.first << ' ' << edge.second << '\n';
    }
    
    return 0;
}

2. **Finding Components**: After processing all existing roads, we determine the connected components using the DSU.
3. **Global Minimum Component**: We identify the component with the smallest house price. This component will act as the central hub.
4. **Connecting Components**: Each component is connected to the global minimum component via the cheapest possible road, ensuring minimal total cost.

This approach ensures that we connect all components with the minimal cost by leveraging the existing roads and adding new roads optimally.

### **Device Design: Portable Live Circuit Breaker Bypass Device (PLC-BBD)**

Below is one example of how you might approach the problem. (Note that any procedure for hot‐swapping high–voltage/current equipment must be vetted by rigorous safety and engineering reviews; the following is a conceptual design meant to illustrate one potential solution.)

──────────────────────────────
1. Replacing a Breaker Without a Power Outage

The basic idea is to use a “make–before–break” procedure. Normally, replacing a circuit breaker involves interrupting the circuit, but if you can temporarily “bridge” the circuit with a bypass device that carries the load while you swap the breaker, you can avoid an outage. In many industrial applications the solution is to use a redundant path or bypass switch (sometimes called a hot–swap module or temporary jumper) that is engaged before the faulty device is removed. For example, you might:

• Install a temporary bypass module that uses high–current contactors connected in parallel with the breaker.
• Engage these contactors “on” first so that the load continues to be energized.
• Once the bypass is confirmed active, remove the faulty breaker and install the replacement.
• Finally, disengage the temporary bypass so that the circuit is once again controlled by a standard breaker device.

This “make–before–break” method requires synchronized actuation (so that the bypass always engages before the breaker is removed), proper insulation, overcurrent protection, and procedures that ensure no open–circuit conditions occur.

──────────────────────────────
2. Checking for Patented Devices

Before designing something new, you’d start with a patent search. Some patents exist for “hot swap circuit breaker” or “transfer switch bypass” modules (or “make–before–break” devices in high–power applications). For example, you might search databases (like the USPTO or Espacenet) for keywords such as “hot swap circuit breaker bypass,” “redundant breaker module,” or “live insertion circuit protection.”  
• Document any prior art that details devices that allow live insertion or removal of circuit protection devices.  
• Confirm which aspects (mechanical interlocks, contactor designs, control algorithms) have been patented.  
• Then decide on novel design features (for instance, unique contact geometry, additional safeguards, or faster microprocessor–based control logic) that distinguish your device.

──────────────────────────────
3. Proposed Design: Hot Swap Breaker Bypass Module

Below is a conceptual design of a device (“Hot Swap Breaker Bypass Module”) intended to allow safe replacement of circuit breakers in critical high–power applications without interrupting power.

A. Functional Overview

• Passive Bypass: The device is a compact, plug–in module that mechanically and electrically bridges the faulty breaker position.
• Make–Before–Break Operation: The device achieves a make–before–break connection using two sets of synchronized contacts. One set is engaged from the “live” side and another on the downstream load side, ensuring the load path is never interrupted.
• Control and Sensing: Integrated sensors, interlock circuits, and a microcontroller ensure that contacts only move once both sides (input and output) are confirmed to be ready, minimizing transient interruption.
• Safety and Fault Detection: Built–in fault monitoring, thermal sensors, and current monitors continuously check that the module is operating within safe limits. In the event of a fault, the module signals an alarm and automatically opens the contacts if needed.
• Redundancy: The design includes redundant circuitry and mechanical interlocks, ensuring that failure of the bypass device itself does not create an open–circuit condition.

B. Major Components/Parts

1. High–Current Synchronized Contact Blocks  
  • Mechanically robust, high–amp rated contacts – similar to those in industrial circuit breakers but designed with a “make–before–break” geometry.  
  • Dual–stage contactors arranged so that the temporary bypass is never disengaged until its replacement circuit breaker is confirmed removed.

2. Electromechanical Actuators with Interlocks  
  • Motorized or solenoid actuators control the linkage between contact blocks.  
  • Mechanical interlock systems (or redundant sensors) ensure that the two contact sets move in a synchronized manner.

3. Control Unit  
  • A microcontroller (with redundant safety software) monitors sensor inputs (voltage, current, contact position, temperature).  
  • It controls the actuators and only permits movement when conditions are safe.  
  • User interface lights (LED indications) and a simple push–button or switch let the operator initiate the bypass sequence.

4. Sensing and Protection Circuits  
  • Voltage and current sensors monitor the downstream and upstream conditions.  
  • Integrated surge suppressors or transient voltage protection (TVS) diodes protect the control circuit.  
  • Thermal sensors detect any overheating in the contact blocks or wiring.

5. Mechanical Housing and Insulation  
  • A ruggedized, dielectric–rated enclosure protects the circuitry and contact mechanisms.  
  • The design meets industrial safety standards with appropriate clearances and creepage distances.

6. Communication/Interface Module (Optional)  
  • For integration with central control systems, an Ethernet, Modbus, or other industrial communication interface can log operations and alarms.

C. Operational Steps

1. Pre–Insertion Check  
  • The operator attaches the bypass module into dedicated slots on the power panel that are designed for live insertion.  
  • The control unit performs a self–diagnosis: It confirms power levels, verifies the readiness of the contact blocks, and checks that the mechanical interlocks are in the proper “engage” position.

2. Bypass Engagement  
  • Once the bypass module is physically in place, the operator initiates the “engage” command.  
  • The control unit actuates the high–current contact blocks in a make–before–break sequence:  
   a. First, the upstream (live) contact block closes, ensuring current still flows to the panel.  
   b. Then, the downstream contact block is closed, completing the temporary bypass circuit.  
  • Status LEDs confirm that the bypass is active and carrying the load current safely.

3. Breaker Replacement  
  • With the bypass active, the faulty circuit breaker is removed and the new circuit breaker is installed.  
  • The bypass module remains engaged, seamlessly bridging the connection without interruption in current flow.

4. Bypass Disengagement and Restoration  
  • After confirming proper installation of the new breaker, the operator initiates a “disengage” command on the bypass module.  
  • The control unit again executes a synchronized “break–before–make” operation that disconnects the bypass safely.  
  • Complete system status is verified, and the bypass module is removed or stowed until the next maintenance event.

──────────────────────────────
4. Safety and Engineering Considerations

• Rigorous Testing: Before fielding such a device, extensive testing (including fault simulation, thermal cycling, and transient analysis) must be performed.  
• Standards Compliance: The design would be reviewed against industrial and electrical safety standards (for example, IEC, UL, IEEE) to ensure safe live insertion and operation under high–power conditions.  
• Redundancy & Fail–Safes: The module must fail in a “closed circuit” or “safe” mode so that its malfunction does not inadvertently open the load circuit.

──────────────────────────────
5. Summary

The proposed Hot Swap Breaker Bypass Module is intended to provide a temporary, electronically controlled high-current path to allow the safe replacement of a circuit breaker in a critical power-distribution panel. In brief:

• A patent search should first be conducted to identify existing solutions and ensure that novel aspects of your design (e.g., contact geometry, control synchronization) are protected.  
• The design utilizes a make–before–break scheme with redundant electromechanical actuators, synchronized high–current contacts, and robust sensing and control electronics.  
• The module’s operation is divided into pre–insertion checks, bypass engagement, breaker replacement, and bypass disengagement—all carried out in a controlled, safe manner to avoid power outages.

This conceptual design is a starting point for a detailed engineering solution that, after thorough prototyping and testing, could enable safe hot–swapping of circuit breakers without disrupting critical power systems.

Here's a robust TypeScript solution that wraps a function in a try/catch block and returns a `Result` type, handling both synchronous and asynchronous operations:

```typescript
type Result<T> =
  | { type: 'success'; value: T }
  | { type: 'error'; error: unknown };

function tryCatch<T extends any[], R>(
  fn: (...args: T) => R
): (...args: T) => Promise<Result<Awaited<R>>> {
  return async (...args: T): Promise<Result<Awaited<R>>> => {
    try {
      const result = fn(...args);
      const value = await result;
      return { type: 'success', value };
    } catch (error) {
      return { type: 'error', error };
    }
  };
}
```

**Key features:**
1. **Unified error handling:** Works with both synchronous and asynchronous functions
2. **Type safety:** Properly infers return types using `Awaited`
3. **Discriminated union:** Clear success/error states with type predicates
4. **Argument forwarding:** Preserves original function parameters

**Usage examples:**

```typescript
// Synchronous function
const syncExample = tryCatch((a: number, b: number) => a + b);
const syncResult = await syncExample(2, 3); // { type: 'success', value: 5 }

// Asynchronous function
const asyncExample = tryCatch(async (url: string) => {
  const response = await fetch(url);
  return response.json();
});
const asyncResult = await asyncExample('https://api.example.com');

// Error handling
if (asyncResult.type === 'success') {
  console.log('Data:', asyncResult.value);
} else {
  console.error('Error:', asyncResult.error);
}
```

**Advantages:**
- Single API for both sync/async operations
- Preserves TypeScript type information
- Simple error checking via type discrimination
- Properly unwraps nested promises
- Maintains original function parameter types

This implementation ensures type safety while providing a clean, modern API for error handling in TypeScript applications.

You have a music player with a library of over 1000 songs with all of them added to a default "All Songs" playlist. You want to listen to a *specific* song, followed by a shuffled playback of all the *other* songs in your library. The challenge is to achieve this using only the following functionalities:

**Music Player Functionalities:**

* **Playlist Shuffle:** Clears the queue (including the currently playing song if any), shuffles the entire "All Songs" playlist, and **adds it to the queue.** This also **always disables Queue Shuffle.**
* **Search:** Allows you to search for specific songs within your library.
* **Queue:** The player maintains a queue of upcoming songs. The queue's content is determined by how a song is initiated for playback:
    * **Playing from Playlist:** The queue mirrors the order of the "All Songs" playlist.
    * **Playing from Search Results:** The queue contains only the songs from the search results.
    * **Important:** If the queue is empty and you add a song using "Play Next," regardless of whether it's from the search results or the playlist, the queue will only contain that single song.
* **Player Shuffle (Queue Shuffle):** Shuffles the remaining songs in the queue *after* the currently playing song. This function is only accessible when there are songs in the queue.
    * **Important:** Queue Shuffle can be toggled ON/OFF independently **at any time.** If toggled ON after songs are added to the queue, it will shuffle them. If toggled OFF after shuffling, the queue retains its shuffled order. Toggling it ON again will re-shuffle the queue.
* **Play Next:** (Available from search results and the playlist) Adds the selected song to the queue, to be played immediately after the currently playing song. This function's behavior is affected by the Queue Shuffle state:
    * **Queue Shuffle OFF:** Adds the song to the top of the queue.
    * **Queue Shuffle ON:** Inserts the song randomly into the queue.
    * **Special Case:** If Queue Shuffle is ON when a song is added via "Play Next," the song will be inserted randomly into the queue. If Queue Shuffle is then toggled OFF, the added song will be moved to the next position in the queue, and the rest of the queue will return to its pre-shuffle order.
* **Next Button:** Skips to the next song in the queue.
* **Stop Player:** Stops the music playback and clears the entire queue. It also disables Queue Shuffle.

**Clarifications:**

* You *must* use the search function to find your specific song.
* "Playlist Shuffle" **clears the existing queue, including the current song, adds the entire shuffled playlist to the queue,** and disables Queue Shuffle.
* After achieving the desired playback order (your specific song first, followed by a shuffled queue), the shuffled portion of the queue *may* contain a duplicate of the song you initially wanted to listen to.
* You can toggle Queue Shuffle ON or OFF at any point during the process.

**The Challenge:**

Can you determine a sequence of actions using only these functionalities to achieve the desired playback: your specific song first, followed by a shuffled playback of all other songs in the library? Remember to consider the impact of the Queue Shuffle toggle and the "Stop Player" function, especially the new information about the behavior of "Play Next" with an empty queue.

**You must also describe the state of the queue after each step.**

(It’s acceptable if the later randomized portion includes your song again.) 

Let’s assume your target song is “Song X.” One valid sequence is as follows:

Read through the recipe completely before beginning.

─────────────────────────────  
1. OVERVIEW & LAYERING  
─────────────────────────────

• You will bake three (≈5 cm–high) white sponge cake rounds using 26 cm round pans.
• You’ll make a light simple syrup to soak the cakes.
• The interior “fillings” are as follows (from bottom upward):
  a) On the bottom cake layer: After soaking, spread a layer of homemade chocolate–hazelnut spread and, over that, scatter a light layer (≈50 g) of homemade feuilletine flakes.
  b) Place the second (middle) sponge cake layer (also soaked) and then spread a generous layer of fruit cream spread (≈500 g total are divided over the cake’s area).

─────────────────────────────

Below is a carefully tested recipe for a 20‐serving white “layered” sponge cake with soaked layers, whipped cream frosting, and three distinct middle “spreads” (a homemade chocolate–hazelnut spread enhanced with baked feuilletine, a fruit cream spread, and a fruit jelly “glaze”). In this recipe you’ll make your own crispy feuilletine flakes (don’t just buy them!), prepare three fillings, and bake three sponge‐cake rounds in 26 cm (10‑inch) diameter pans. Read through the recipe completely before beginning.

─────────────────────────────  
1. OVERVIEW & LAYERING  
─────────────────────────────

• You will bake three (≈5 cm–high) white sponge cake rounds using 26 cm round pans.
• You’ll make a light simple syrup to soak the cakes.
• The interior “fillings” are as follows (from bottom upward):
  a) On the bottom cake layer: After soaking, spread a layer of homemade chocolate–hazelnut spread and, over that, scatter a light layer (≈50 g) of homemade feuilletine flakes.
  b) Place the second (middle) sponge cake layer (also soaked) and then spread a generous layer of fruit cream spread (≈500 g total are divided over the cake’s area).
  c) Place the top (third) sponge round, then “glaze” the top by brushing on a thin, uneven covering (≈250 g total) of fruit jelly (we suggest a tangy passion‐fruit jelly for contrast).
• Finally, frost the entire exterior with a light whipped cream frosting. (If desired, you can also gently “curtain” a little extra feuilletine and add some fresh fruit slices on top for garnish.)

─────────────────────────────  
2. INGREDIENTS  
─────────────────────────────

A. White Sponge Cake (3 rounds in 26 cm pans)  
• Large eggs, at room temperature: 10 eggs  
• Granulated sugar: 250 g  
• All‐purpose flour, sifted: 250 g  
• Salt: ¼ tsp  
• Vanilla extract: 1 tsp  
• Unsalted butter, melted and cooled: 100 g  

B. Simple Syrup (for soaking)  
• Granulated sugar: 100 g  
• Water: 100 ml

C. Homemade Chocolate–Hazelnut Spread  
(Blend these until smooth; yield ≈400–450 g)  
• Toasted hazelnuts (skins rubbed off), finely ground: 100 g  
• Milk chocolate (at about 40–45% cocoa content), chopped: 200 g  
• Unsalted butter, melted: 50 g  
• Powdered sugar, sifted: 50 g  
• A pinch of salt

D. Homemade Feuilletine (for crisp “flakes”)  
(You will make a thin, caramelized wafer, then break it by hand into irregular flakes; yield ~150 g)  
• Unsalted butter, melted: 100 g  
• Granulated sugar: 150 g  
• All‐purpose flour: 120 g  
• A pinch of salt  
• (You will spread the mixture very thin–about 2–3 mm–on a 30×40 cm baking sheet.)

E. Fruit Cream Spread (Strawberry Style)  
(You want a smooth, creamy, fruit‐tinted filling; yield ≈500 g)  
• Mascarpone cheese: 250 g  
• Fresh strawberries, pureed and sieved (or high‐quality strawberry puree): 100 g  
• Powdered sugar, sifted: 50 g  
• Heavy cream (30% fat), chilled: 150 g (whipped to soft peaks; see “Whipped Cream” below)  

F. Fruit Jelly (Passion‐Fruit Flavor)  
(Spreadable, not too stiff; yield ≈250 g)  
• Passion‐fruit pulp (from fresh or good quality pulp, strained): 200 g  
• Granulated sugar: 100 g  
• Water: 100 ml  
• Agar agar powder: 3 g  
  Note: (If you prefer gelatin, you could use about 6 g, dissolved in a little water, but agar agar sets more sharply and gives a clear jelly.)  

G. Whipped Cream Frosting  
• Heavy cream (35% fat), chilled: 400 ml  
• Powdered sugar, sifted: 50 g  
• Vanilla extract: 1 tsp

─────────────────────────────  
3. PREPARATIONS  
─────────────────────────────

A. White Sponge Cake  
1. Preheat your oven to 180°C (350°F). Grease three 26 cm round cake pans and line the bottoms with parchment paper.
2. In a large bowl, beat the 10 eggs and 250 g granulated sugar with an electric mixer on high speed for about 8–10 minutes until the mixture becomes tripled in volume and pale.
3. Sift together 250 g flour and ¼ tsp salt. Gently fold the flour into the egg mixture using a spatula. Add the 1 tsp vanilla extract.
4. Gently fold in the melted butter (ensure it is not hot) until just incorporated.
5. Divide the batter evenly among the three pans. Bake for 25–30 minutes or until a skewer inserted in the center comes out clean.
6. Cool the cakes in the pans for 10 minutes, then transfer to a wire rack to cool completely.

B. Simple Syrup  
1. In a small saucepan combine 100 g sugar and 100 ml water. Bring to a boil and let simmer for 2 minutes until the sugar completely dissolves. Remove from heat and let cool to room temperature.

C. Homemade Feuilletine  
1. Preheat your oven to 200°C (392°F). Line a 30×40 cm baking sheet with parchment paper.
2. In a bowl, whisk together 100 g melted unsalted butter, 150 g granulated sugar, 120 g flour, and a pinch of salt until you have a smooth and fairly loose batter.
3. Spread the mixture very thinly (2–3 mm thickness) over the parchment paper.
4. Bake for about 10–12 minutes. Look for a deep golden color and a crispy texture.
5. Remove from the oven and allow to cool completely. Once cool, break the baked wafer into irregular “feuilletine” flakes by hand; you should collect about 150 g of flakes in total.

D. Homemade Chocolate–Hazelnut Spread  
1. In a heatproof bowl, melt the 200 g chopped milk chocolate (you may use a microwave in 20‑second bursts or a double boiler) and then stir in the 50 g melted butter.
2. In a food processor, combine the 100 g toasted hazelnuts, 50 g powdered sugar, and a pinch of salt. Pulse to finely grind (but not to a paste).
3. Add the warm chocolate–butter mixture to the hazelnut powder and blend until smooth. Taste and adjust if needed.
4. (Allow the spread to come to room temperature before using; it should be spreadable.)

E. Fruit Cream Spread  
1. In a medium bowl, mix the 250 g mascarpone with 50 g powdered sugar.
2. Stir in the 100 g strawberry puree gently until blended.
3. In a separate bowl, whip 150 g heavy cream to soft peaks.
4. Fold the whipped cream into the mascarpone mixture very gently until you have a homogenous, airy cream.

F. Fruit Jelly (Passion‐Fruit)  
1. In a small saucepan, combine 100 g granulated sugar and 100 ml water. Bring to a boil.
2. Add 200 g passion‐fruit pulp and 3 g agar agar. Stir continuously and let simmer for about 2 minutes so that the agar agar dissolves thoroughly.
3. Remove from heat and allow the mixture to cool slightly (it will thicken as it cools but must remain spreadable and not firm like a fully set gel). If using gelatin instead, follow the package directions for blooming and dissolving.
   
G. Whipped Cream Frosting  
1. Place 400 ml heavy cream in a chilled bowl. Add 50 g powdered sugar and 1 tsp vanilla extract.
2. Whip until stiff peaks form. (Do not overwhip; the frosting should be light and smooth.)

─────────────────────────────  
4. ASSEMBLY  
─────────────────────────────

Note: If you prefer to assemble the cake a day in advance, wrap it loosely in plastic wrap and chill; let it sit at room temperature about 30 minutes before serving so that the layers soften slightly and the flavors meld.

A. Level each sponge cake if necessary.
B. Using a serrated knife, trim a very thin layer from the top of each cake to create flat surfaces.

C. Assemble in a 26 cm cake stand or large serving platter:

  1. Place the first (bottom) sponge cake layer.
     – Immediately brush the top evenly with about 1/3–1/2 of the simple syrup.
     – Spread the entire surface with the homemade chocolate–hazelnut spread (approximately 300 g total, i.e. about 2/3 of the prepared spread) using an offset spatula.
     – Evenly scatter roughly 50 g of the feuilletine flakes over the chocolate–hazelnut layer. (The crispy feuilletine will add texture that contrasts nicely with the other silky spreads.)

  2. Gently set the second (middle) sponge cake layer on top.
     – Brush its top with another 1/3–1/2 of the syrup.
     – Spread the fruit cream spread evenly over this second layer (use all or most of the 500 g prepared; smooth out to about a 2–3 cm thickness).
    
  3. Place the top (third) sponge cake layer.
     – Brush the top with the remaining simple syrup.
     – While still slightly warm (or at room temperature), gently “glaze” the top with the passion‐fruit jelly. Use a thin spatula or pastry brush to achieve an uneven, artisanal look using about 250 g of jelly. (If you prefer, you may also let the jelly set into a “mirror‐glaze” style.)
    
  4. Finally, frost the entire exterior (sides and top) with the whipped cream frosting. Use an offset spatula or a piping bag for a neat finish.
     – Optionally, sprinkle a few extra feuilletine flakes (≈50 g) over the top and decorate with fresh strawberry slices (or other complementary fruits) for added color and texture.

─────────────────────────────  
5. NOTES  
─────────────────────────────

• Work gently when folding ingredients so that you keep the batter and cream light.
• Accurate weighing is key: Use a digital scale for all ingredients.
• The 26 cm pans are chosen because a cake this size (with three layers, each roughly 5 cm tall before trimming) will serve 20 generously.
• You can adjust the fruit flavors: Replace strawberry puree in the cream spread with raspberry or even a mix of berries, and vary the fruit jelly flavor (mango or kiwi would also be lovely with the chocolate–hazelnut spread).
• When baking the feuilletine, watch closely because oven temperatures vary; you want a crisp, golden wafer that breaks easily into flakes.
• Assemble and chill the cake for a few hours (or overnight) to allow flavors to meld and for the layers to firm up for easier slicing.

─────────────────────────────  
Enjoy!  
─────────────────────────────

This recipe yields a show‐stopping cake full of layers, textures, and flavors—from the delicacy of the sponge and whipped cream ﬁrst, to the crunch of feuilletine intermingled with nutty chocolate, fresh fruit cream, and a tangy passion‐fruit jelly finish. Happy baking!

judgment.answer:
## My own answer

Given the user’s requirements—training a draft/draft-building bot on only which cards appear together (no meta data, no drafts, only decklists, not even considering mana costs, card colors, types), and with particular handling for basic lands—here’s my plan and what the script should do:

**Algorithm/Approach:**

- **Training step:**  
  - Parse all historical deck files.
  - For each deck, count the number of copies for each non-basic card. Build:
    - A co-occurrence matrix: For each card pair in a deck (including duplicates), increment the pair's counter by (copies_A × copies_B).  
    - For total appearances: For each card, sum up how many times it appears (across all decks, including duplicates).
    - For basics balance: Collect the average ratio/distribution of each basic land used across decks, but do *not* use basics for co-occurrences or total counts.

- **During a draft:**
  - Read the relevant .json log file.
  - On each pack, for every card offered:
      - If any of the already-picked cards has a nonzero co-occurrence with the offered card, sum all such co-occurrences as its "score".
      - If none, use the total appearance count as fallback (with 'A' prefix).
      - Present the cards in a sorted fashion as described.

- **Deckbuilding:**
  - Once picks are done: Use all picked non-basic cards in the deck, no cutting.
  - For basic lands, fill remaining slots (to 40 total) according to the trained basics ratio/proportion.

- **UI:**
  - Tkinter UI, always-on-top.

- **Additional notes:**
  - Card ids/names are matched via a lookup file.
  - Decks may have multiple copies of a card, which must affect co-occurrences.
  - Only non-basic lands considered for picks and co-occurrences. Basics used only for filling out the deck and for land balancing.

**Outline of code/components:**
- Training phase: read all decks, populate co-occurrence matrix, appearances counter, and basics ratio.
- Read in id-to-name mapping.
- Tkinter GUI:
  - On update (triggered by timer or filewatch): parse current draft state, picks, and current pack.
  - For each pack card, get name, skip basics, compute score vs picks, sort and display.
  - Build-deck button: uses all picked non-basics, fill up with basics according to trained land ratios.
- Always-on-top behaviour via Tkinter attribute.

**Important details:**
- Multiples of the same card both in the same deck, and with respect to draft picks, are counted.
- When filling up lands, if rounding creates a mismatch, should distribute/reduce from the highest fraction.

---

## Now, evaluation

### Assistant A

- **Adheres to requirements?** Yes; script matches all requested logic.
- **Structure & walkthrough:** Provides a thorough walk-through, dividing the code into sections—training, mapping, live draft reading, suggestions, deckbuilding, UI.
- **Code:** 
  - Deck processing parses quantities, correctly accounts for copy numbers for co-occurrence and frequency.
  - Co-occurrence: computes (copies_A * copies_B) for each card-pair in a deck.
  - Per-deck land proportions are computed and averaged for final basics ratios.
  - Draft updates tie picks/suggestions to current pool, presenting scores (co-occurrence sum, or ‘A’ for appearances).
  - Deck-building keeps all non-basic picks, fills up to 40 with basics by average ratio learned from decks. If picked non-basics > 40, truncates arbitrarily (possibly a weak spot, but that’s a rare case).
  - UI is Tkinter, always-on-top, manual “Build Final Deck” option.
- **Clarity:** Thorough explanations before and after code.
- **Completeness:** All pieces present—training, card id mapping, live update, deckbuilding, UI, path configs. Logic is correct per requirements.
- **Possible improvements:** Maybe a little verbose, but nothing is superfluous. Truncating non-basics > 40 is handled with a warning.

### Assistant B

- **Adheres to requirements?** Largely yes, but a few problems:
  - The script calculates a "land-data" breakdown *per non-basic card* (i.e., for each non-basic card, how many of each land were in its decks), then uses this to estimate land distribution for a recommended deck, instead of calculating global average land proportions. This introduces a more complex mechanism than requested.
  - Also, shows “recommendedDeck” from the draft log (which is not relevant—the user's bot should suggest *from the pool picked during this draft*, not from the game's own recommendations).
- **Code:**
  - Overall structure similar, but training builds per-card land associations—which isn’t what user asks (user wants *total* land ratios from decks, not *per-card*).
  - In deckbuilding, lands are calculated using weighted averages from non-basic cards’ land usage, which is not what the user describes/wants.
  - The UI auto-pops up the recommended deck in a messagebox *each time the draft updates*, which might be a problem if you're picking—should only prompt at end, or on user request.
  - Co-occurrence is only checked for picked card names (duplicates in picked list): code gets picks from all previous picks (including repeated cards, which is correct).
  - The pack's cards are sorted; for scoring, the mix is mostly correct (falling back to 'A' for total appearances), but sorting is less precise (sorts all by int(x[0].strip('A')), which may put fallback and real-synergy in the same level).
- **Clarity:** Explanations are clear, but details of how land is calculated don't fully match user instructions.
- **Completeness:** The core draft suggestion algorithm is there, but some logic deviates from the strict requirements; the deckbuilding step is more intricate than necessary and arguably less correct per requirements.
- **Possible improvements:** Land calculation should be fixed to average the basic land ratios globally, not per-card. Showing final decklist should be user-triggered, not auto. Sorting could better separate cards with zero and nonzero synergy.

---

### Comparison to my model answer:

- **Co-occurrence and frequencies:** Both handle these correctly.
- **Basic lands handling:** Assistant A does *average across decks* as user requires; Assistant B builds per-card land averages, which is a deviation and may not produce appropriate basics ratios in the context of best-practice deckbuilding, especially as per the user's requirements (which explicitly wants *not* to consider color or mana associations).
- **Deckbuilding:** Assistant A fills using fixed globally-trained basic ratios; Assistant B does not.
- **UI:** Both are always-on-top, however, Assistant A's UI is more user-driven and detailed. Assistant B triggers deck recommendation as a popup automatically, which could be annoying.
- **Presentation and code:** Assistant A is longer, but for good reason—covers all the details and is more robust.

### Final details

- *Missing information in B:* B does not compute basics ratios per user instructions; it might produce lands according to cards' land "neighborhood", which is not what was requested. Also, the unsolicited use of recommendedDeck from drafts.json is unnecessary, as the user wants to build the final deck based off the pool of cards the user picked, using the co-occurrence or frequencies, with optimal basic lands.
- *Novelty/creativity:* Neither is particularly creative (by design—the task is procedural), but Assistant A is more strictly accurate and precisely implements what is asked.

## Final Verdict

Assistant A more completely and correctly implements the solution requested, including every algorithmic aspect specifically requested in the prompt, whereas Assistant B deviates from requirements in a couple of core respects.

**Therefore:**
[[A>>B]]

Below is one example of a combined Python script that “trains” on your past 7‑0 decks (ignoring everything except which non‐basic cards tend to appear together, and also keeping a total‐frequency count) and then launches a simple always‐on‑top Tkinter window that:

• reads a live JSON file with your draft state,
• matches card IDs to names,
• computes a “synergy score” for each offered card (by summing how many times it “co‑occurred” in training with every card you’ve already picked),
• and, if a candidate has zero synergy then it falls back to showing the total frequency (prefixed with an “A” as requested).

When the draft ends (or when you hit a “Build Deck” button) the script “builds” a final deck from your drafted pool plus a computed balance of basic lands. In this example the basic‐land balance is computed from your training decks (by reading their basic–land counts) so that their relative proportions (Forest, Mountain, Island, Plains, Swamp) follow (roughly) the averages from your training data, and the number of lands is simply chosen to “fill” the deck to 40 cards.

For clarity the script is divided into several sections:
 1. TRAINING: It loads every “deck” text file from your deck folder (ignoring basic lands except when counting basic–land ratios) and builds 
  a. a co‑occurrence “matrix” (a nested dict with frequencies that are multiplied by card copy counts) and 
  b. a “total frequency” dictionary (again using copy counts)
  c. plus it computes basic–land ratios from those decks.
 2. ID MAPPING: It loads your mtga IDs file (which maps numbers like “91029” to card names).
 3. LIVE DRAFT READING AND PICK SUGGESTION: It polls your draft json file repeatedly (every few seconds) and, if it finds a draft “pick” in progress, it computes for every card in the current pack a pick “score” (by summing, for every already‑picked card, the co‑occurrence frequency from training). If that score is zero then it shows instead the “A” plus the candidate’s overall frequency.
 4. FINAL DECK RECOMMENDATION: When you trigger it (with a button) it “builds” a final deck. Here the simplest logic is used – it takes your drafted cards (with the correct multiplicitiy) and then computes how many extra cards are needed to total 40; then it applies the basic–land ratios from training to “fill” the remaining slots.
 5. UI: A Tkinter window that is set “always on top” so it won’t be hidden by your MTG Arena window.

Below is one complete (self‑contained) script. (You’ll likely have to adjust paths and perhaps tweak parameters.)

#!/usr/bin/env python
"""
MTG Arena Draft Assistant Bot
Author: (Your Name)
Date: (Today’s Date)

This script trains on a folder of winning MTG Arena decks (from 17lands) by considering only which
non‐basic cards tend to occur together. It then launches an always‐on‐top Tkinter UI which polls the live
draft log (drafts.json) and, using the training data and a mapping of card IDs to names, suggests pick
priorities sorted in order of synergy with already’drafted cards. When you hit “Build Final Deck”
the bot computes a final recommended 40‑card deck including a “balanced” count of basic lands determined
from the training decks.
"""

import os
import json
import threading
import time
from collections import defaultdict
import tkinter as tk
from tkinter import scrolledtext

# -------------- CONFIGURATION --------------

# Folder with deck txt files from 17lands (each file is a deck)
DECKS_FOLDER = r"C:\Users\Braiks\Downloads\ManualMH3Decks"

# File mapping card IDs to card names (comma‐separated values – first token is the id)
IDS_FILE = r"C:\Users\Braiks\Downloads\mtga bot\mh3ids.txt"

# Live draft JSON file (updated by your MTG Arena utility)
DRAFTS_JSON = r"C:\Users\Braiks\AppData\Roaming\untapped-companion\drafts.json"

# Basic land names (exact match; any card with exactly one of these names is considered “a basic”)
BASIC_LANDS = {"Forest", "Mountain", "Island", "Plains", "Swamp"}

# Total deck size (includes basic lands)
TOTAL_DECK_SIZE = 40

# Polling interval for draft JSON (seconds)
POLL_INTERVAL = 3

# -------------- TRAINING FUNCTIONS --------------

def train_on_decks(decks_folder):
    """
    Scan all txt deck files in decks_folder.
    For each deck file, parse each line into a (quantity, card name) pair.
    Build:
     - co_occurrence: dict[card][other_card] = sum over decks (copies(card)*copies(other_card))
     - total_frequency: dict[card] = total copies in all decks
     - basics_ratio: average ratio (across decks) for each basic land.
       (Note: decks contain basic lands; we use lines with exactly a basic land name.)
    """
    co_occurrence = defaultdict(lambda: defaultdict(int))
    total_frequency = defaultdict(int)
    # For computing basic lands proportion:
    total_basics = defaultdict(int)
    total_non_basic_cards = 0
    deck_count = 0

    # Loop over all .txt files in the folder
    for filename in os.listdir(decks_folder):
        if not filename.lower().endswith(".txt"):
            continue
        deck_count += 1
        filepath = os.path.join(decks_folder, filename)
        with open(filepath, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
            deck_cards = {}  # card name -> count
            deck_basics = defaultdict(int)
            for line in f:
                line = line.strip()
                if not line:
                    continue
                # Expecting a line like: "9 Plains" or "1 Sundering Eruption"
                try:
                    qty_str, cardname = line.split(" ", 1)
                    qty = int(qty_str)
                except Exception as ex:
                    print(f"Error parsing line [{line}] in {filename}: {ex}")
                    continue
                if cardname in BASIC_LANDS:
                    deck_basics[cardname] += qty
                else:
                    deck_cards[cardname] = deck_cards.get(cardname, 0) + qty
                    total_frequency[cardname] += qty

            # Update co-occurrence: for every ordered pair (A, B) in deck_cards,
            # add (copies_A * copies_B). (Note: will count both A->B and B->A.)
            cards = list(deck_cards.items())
            for i in range(len(cards)):
                cardA, countA = cards[i]
                for j in range(len(cards)):
                    cardB, countB = cards[j]
                    # You might want to skip when A==B if you prefer—but since copies matter,
                    # counting self-pairs can be meaningful.
                    co_occurrence[cardA][cardB] += countA * countB

            # For basics ratios:
            non_basic_count = sum(deck_cards.values())
            total_non_basic_cards += non_basic_count
            for basic in BASIC_LANDS:
                total_basics[basic] += deck_basics.get(basic, 0)

    # Compute average ratio for each basic land: avg basic count per deck divided by average non-basic count.
    basics_ratio = {}
    if deck_count > 0 and total_non_basic_cards > 0:
        avg_non_basic = total_non_basic_cards / deck_count
        for basic in BASIC_LANDS:
            avg_basic = total_basics[basic] / deck_count
            # Save ratio: fraction of basic lands relative to non-basics.
            basics_ratio[basic] = avg_basic / avg_non_basic if avg_non_basic > 0 else 0
    else:
        # Fallback: equal distribution.
        for basic in BASIC_LANDS:
            basics_ratio[basic] = 1.0 / len(BASIC_LANDS)
    print("Training complete. Processed {} decks.".format(deck_count))
    return co_occurrence, total_frequency, basics_ratio

# -------------- ID MAPPING --------------

def load_card_ids(ids_file):
    """
    Load a mapping of card_id (as string) to card name.
    Each line is expected to be like: "91029, Conduit Goblin"
    (comma may be present inside the card name, but the first comma separates the id).
    """
    id_to_name = {}
    try:
        with open(ids_file, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
            for line in f:
                line = line.strip()
                if not line:
                    continue
                # Split at first comma.
                parts = line.split(",", 1)
                if len(parts) != 2:
                    continue
                card_id = parts[0].strip()
                card_name = parts[1].strip()
                id_to_name[card_id] = card_name
    except Exception as ex:
        print("Error loading card IDs:", ex)
    print("Loaded {} card IDs.".format(len(id_to_name)))
    return id_to_name

# -------------- DRAFT STATE AND PICK SUGGESTION --------------

def get_current_draft_state(drafts_json_file):
    """
    Read the current draft state from the drafts.json file.
    This function loads the JSON and (naively) picks the first draft that is in progress.
    Returns a tuple: (draft_id, current_pack (list of card ids), picked_cards (list of card ids))
    If nothing is found, returns (None, None, None).
    Note: In the provided JSON snippet, "DraftStatus":"Draft.PickNext" signals a pick in progress.
    """
    try:
        with open(drafts_json_file, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
            data = json.load(f)
    except Exception as ex:
        print("Error loading draft json:", ex)
        return None, None, None

    # Look for a draft that has at least one pick with DraftStatus "Draft.PickNext"

    with already picked cards. We compute:
         score = sum_over_picked { co_occurrence[card_name(picked)][card_name(candidate)] }
    If the score is zero, we fallback to showing "A" + total frequency (of the candidate card from training).
    Return a list of tuples: (card_id, card_name, score, fallback_flag, fallback_value)

    suggestions = []

    picked_names = [id_to_name.get(cid, f"Unknown({cid})") for cid in picked_cards]

    First, the non-basic cards come from the drafted pool (multiplicity is kept).
    Then, compute the number of basic lands required to reach TOTAL_DECK_SIZE.
    Distribute the basic lands in proportion to basics_ratio.

    in the "draft" portion.

    deck = defaultdict(int)
    non_basic_count = 0
    for cid in drafted_ids:
        card_name = id_to_name.get(cid, f"Unknown({cid})")
        # Skip if the card is one of the five basic lands

        deck[card_name] += 1
        non_basic_count += 1

    basics_needed = TOTAL_DECK_SIZE - non_basic_count
    if basics_needed < 0:
        print("Warning: drafted non-basic cards exceed deck size; truncating non-basics.")
        # In this case, simply keep highest–synergy non-basic cards (here, arbitrarily trim the pool)
        # For now, we'll simply take the first TOTAL_DECK_SIZE cards.
        truncated_deck = {}
        count = 0
        for card, qty in deck.items():
            if count >= TOTAL_DECK_SIZE:
                break
            take = min(qty, TOTAL_DECK_SIZE - count)
            truncated_deck[card] = take
            count += take
        return truncated_deck

    # Distribute basics based on the trained ratios.
    basics_deck = {}
    # First, compute total of ratios for normalization.
    total_ratio = sum(basics_ratio.get(b, 0) for b in BASIC_LANDS)
    for basic in BASIC_LANDS:
        # Compute a preliminary count.
        count = round(basics_needed * (basics_ratio.get(basic, 0)) / total_ratio) if total_ratio > 0 else basics_needed // len(BASIC_LANDS)
        basics_deck[basic] = count
    # Adjust if rounding makes a difference:
    current_basics = sum(basics_deck.values())
    diff = basics_needed - current_basics
    basics_list = list(BASIC_LANDS)
    idx = 0
    while diff != 0:
        b = basics_list[idx % len(basics_list)]
        basics_deck[b] += 1 if diff > 0 else -1
        diff += -1 if diff > 0 else 1
        idx += 1

    # Merge non-basics and basics.
    final_deck = dict(deck)
    for basic, count in basics_deck.items():

def train_on_decks(decks_folder):
    """

     - co_occurrence: dict[card][other_card] = sum over decks (copies(card)*copies(other_card))
     - total_frequency: dict[card] = total copies in all decks
     - basics_ratio: average ratio (across decks) for each basic land.

    co_occurrence = defaultdict(lambda: defaultdict(int))
    total_frequency = defaultdict(int)
    # For computing basic lands proportion:

    total_non_basic_cards = 0
    deck_count = 0

                    total_frequency[cardname] += qty

            # Update co-occurrence: for every ordered pair (A, B) in deck_cards,
            # add (copies_A * copies_B). (Note: will count both A->B and B->A.)
            cards = list(deck_cards.items())
            for i in range(len(cards)):

                for j in range(len(cards)):
                    cardB, countB = cards[j]
                    # You might want to skip when A==B if you prefer—but since copies matter,
                    # counting self-pairs can be meaningful.
                    co_occurrence[cardA][cardB] += countA * countB

            # For basics ratios:

for line in io.lines("input.txt") do
  table.insert(grid, line)
end
local H = #grid
local W = #grid[1]

-- Direction vectors: right, left, down, up
local DIRS = { {0,1}, {0,-1}, {1,0}, {-1,0} }

-- Use string keys for visited states: row..","..col..","..dx..","..dy

local energized = {}
for i=1,H do energized[i]={} end

local queue = {}
local function enqueue(r,c,dx,dy)
  local key = table.concat({r,c,dx,dy}, ",")
  if not visited[key] then
    visited[key] = true
    table.insert(queue, {r=r, c=c, dx=dx, dy=dy})
  end
end

-- Start: (1,1), right direction (dx=0,dy=1)
enqueue(1, 1, 0, 1)

while #queue > 0 do
  local s = table.remove(queue)
  local r, c, dx, dy = s.r, s.c, s.dx, s.dy
  if r<1 or c<1 or r>H or c>W then goto continue end
  energized[r][c] = true

  local cell = grid[r]:sub(c,c)
  if cell == "." then
    enqueue(r+dx, c+dy, dx, dy)
  elseif cell == "/" then
    -- Reflect: switch dx and dy, reverse one
    -- "/" : right (0,1)->up (-1,0), left (0,-1)->down (1,0), up (-1,0)->right (0,1), down (1,0)->left (0,-1)
    enqueue(r - dy, c - dx, -dy, -dx)
  elseif cell == "\\" then
    -- Reflect: switch dx and dy
    -- "\" : right (0,1)->down (1,0), left (0,-1)->up (-1,0), up (-1,0)->left (0,-1), down (1,0)->right (0,1)
    enqueue(r + dy, c + dx, dy, dx)
  elseif cell == "|" then
    -- Pointy ends vertical, flat side from left/right
    if dx == 0 then
      -- Moving horizontally, pass through
      enqueue(r + dx, c + dy, dx, dy)
    else
      -- Moving vertically, split left and right
      enqueue(r, c -1, 0, -1)
      enqueue(r, c +1, 0, 1)
    end
  elseif cell == "-" then
    -- Pointy ends horizontal, flat side from up/down
    if dy == 0 then
      -- Moving vertically, pass through
      enqueue(r + dx, c + dy, dx, dy)
    else
      -- Moving horizontally, split up and down
      enqueue(r - 1, c, -1, 0)
      enqueue(r + 1, c, 1, 0)
    end
  end

end

-- Count energized cells
local count = 0
for r=1,H do

  end
end

    error("Could not open " .. filename)

  for line in f:lines() do

  end

  return grid
end

-- Reflection for mirrors.
local function reflectMirror(ch, dx, dy)
  -- For mirror '/', the mapping is:
  --   right (0,1)  -> up   (-1,0)
  --   left  (0,-1) -> down (1,0)
  --   down  (1,0)  -> left (0,-1)
  --   up    (-1,0) -> right(0,1)
  --
  -- For mirror '\' the mapping is:
  --   right (0,1)  -> down (1,0)
  --   left  (0,-1) -> up   (-1,0)
  --   down  (1,0)  -> right(0,1)
  --   up    (-1,0) -> left (0,-1)
  if ch == '/' then
    if dx == 0 and dy == 1 then
      return -1, 0
    elseif dx == 0 and dy == -1 then
      return 1, 0
    elseif dx == 1 and dy == 0 then
      return 0, -1
    elseif dx == -1 and dy == 0 then
      return 0, 1
    end
  elseif ch == '\\' then
    if dx == 0 and dy == 1 then
      return 1, 0
    elseif dx == 0 and dy == -1 then
      return -1, 0
    elseif dx == 1 and dy == 0 then
      return 0, 1
    elseif dx == -1 and dy == 0 then
      return 0, -1
    end
  end
  -- If something unexpected then just keep going.
  return dx, dy
end

-- Check if a position is inside the grid.
local function inBounds(r, c, height, width)
  return r >= 1 and r <= height and c >= 1 and c <= width
end

-- Main simulation function.
local function simulate(grid)
  local height = #grid
  local width = #grid[1]

  local energized = {}
  for i = 1, height do
    energized[i] = {}
    for j = 1, width do
      energized[i][j] = false
    end
  end

  -- A state is a beam at position (r,c) with direction (dx,dy).
  local beams = {}         -- queue of beams, each beam is {r, c, dx, dy}
  local queueIndex = 1

  -- Use a set to remember visited states to avoid infinite loops.
  local visited = {}

  -- Helper: make a key string for beam state.
  local function stateKey(r, c, dx, dy)
    return r .. "," .. c .. "," .. dx .. "," .. dy
  end

  -- Enqueue a new beam only if not visited already.
  local function enqueue(r, c, dx, dy)
    local key = stateKey(r, c, dx, dy)
    if not visited[key] then

    end
    visited[key] = true

    if inBounds(r, c, height, width) then
      energized[r][c] = true
    end

    -- Get the current cell type.
    if not inBounds(r, c, height, width) then
      -- Beam is out of bounds.
      goto continue
    end
    local cell = grid[r]:sub(c,c)

    if cell == '.' then
      -- Empty tile. Continue on same path.
      local nr, nc = r + dx, c + dy
      if inBounds(nr, nc, height, width) then
        enqueue(nr, nc, dx, dy)
      end

    elseif cell == '/' or cell == '\\' then
      -- Mirror: reflect beam and go on.
      local ndx, ndy = reflectMirror(cell, dx, dy)
      local nr, nc = r + ndx, c + ndy
      if inBounds(nr, nc, height, width) then
        enqueue(nr, nc, ndx, ndy)
      end

    elseif cell == '|' or cell == '-' then
      -- Splitter.
      -- For a vertical splitter ('|'), the pointy (pass‐through) ends are left/right.
      --   So if the beam is moving horizontally (dx==0) it is pointy => no splitting.
      --   If moving vertically (dy==0) then the beam hits the flat side and splits
      --   into beams going left and right.
      -- For a horizontal splitter ('-'), the pointy ends are up/down.
      --   So if the beam moves vertically (dy==0), it passes through; if horizontally,
      --   then it splits into upward and downward moving beams.
      if cell == '|' then
        if dx == 0 and (dy == 1 or dy == -1) then
          -- Pointy side: pass through unchanged.
          local nr, nc = r + dx, c + dy
          if inBounds(nr, nc, height, width) then
            enqueue(nr, nc, dx, dy)
          end
        else
          -- Flat side: split into two beams: left and right.
          local dirs = {{0, -1}, {0, 1}}
          for _, d in ipairs(dirs) do
            local ndx, ndy = d[1], d[2]
            local nr, nc = r + ndx, c + ndy
            if inBounds(nr, nc, height, width) then
              enqueue(nr, nc, ndx, ndy)
            end
          end
        end
      elseif cell == '-' then
        if dy == 0 and (dx == 1 or dx == -1) then
          -- Pointy side: beam goes straight.
          local nr, nc = r + dx, c + dy
          if inBounds(nr, nc, height, width) then
            enqueue(nr, nc, dx, dy)
          end
        else
          -- Horizontal splitter hit on flat side: split into up and down beams.
          local dirs = {{-1, 0}, {1, 0}}
          for _, d in ipairs(dirs) do
            local ndx, ndy = d[1], d[2]

            end
          end
        end

    end

    end

import inspect

import os
import collections.abc

Below is one approach—a series of interconnected, prompt-engineering steps—that you could use to transform a long Discovery call transcript into a set of well-defined, independent user stories. Each step is designed so that its output serves as enriched context for the next prompt, allowing large language models (LLMs) to handle the overall complexity piece by piece.

─────────────────────────────  
Step 1. Preprocess and Segment the Transcript

• Objective: Break the long transcript into manageable segments.  
• What to do:
 – Ask the LLM to scan the transcript and identify natural breaks (e.g., changes in topics, speakers, or technical discussions).  
 – Generate a summary outline that marks sections or “scenes” of the conversation.
• Example Prompt:  
 "Below is a section of a Discovery call transcript. Please identify natural segments or sections in the narrative along with brief summaries of the topics discussed in each segment. This will help us later cluster related requirements."  
• Output Benefit: Provides a roadmap of the discussion so that subsequent analysis isn’t overwhelmed by the transcript’s length.

─────────────────────────────  
Step 2. Extract High-Level Themes and Requirements

• Objective: Identify the main topics, ideas, and potential areas of functionality discussed in the transcript.
• What to do:
 – Use the segmented sections from Step 1 along with any additional context (e.g., known domain details) to prompt the LLM to list high-level themes.
 – This should include functional areas, primary stakeholder concerns, and tentative requirements.
• Example Prompt:

Each story should be independent, focused, and narrow enough to be completed within a sprint. Also, indicate initial acceptance criteria if possible."

─────────────────────────────

 – Provide the candidate user stories (from Step 5) as input and ask the LLM to scrutinize each for clarity, independence, and adherence to business value.

─────────────────────────────  
Step 7. Validate and Iterate with Stakeholder Context

• Objective: Verify that the extracted requirements reflect the original intent of the discovery meeting and align with stakeholder priorities.
• What to do:

Highlight any potential gaps or areas that may require further clarification from the clients."

─────────────────────────────  
Additional Tips

• Context Enrichment: At each step, include snippets from the transcript and additional clarifying context (such as known business goals or user personas) to guide the LLM output.
• Incremental Confirmation: Validate the outputs of each stage with a human subject matter expert before moving to the next step.
• Iterative Improvement: Recognize that some steps may need to be revisited. For example, if emerging user stories are too large or vague, loop back to the functionality extraction or epic grouping steps.

─────────────────────────────  
In Summary

By breaking down the process into these simple, iterative steps—starting from segmentation, moving to themes, drilling down functionalities, organizing epics, then generating and refining user stories—you create a structured pipeline where each prompt builds on the previous one. ```

Story ID | Blocks | Blocked By | Parallelizable With

Sprint Candidate | RICE Score | Risk Factors  
-----------------|------------|--------------

- Ambiguity index per story

**1. Context Extraction & Problem Framing**  
*Prompt Input:* Raw transcript + domain glossary  
*Task:* Identify core business objectives, pain points, and success metrics  
*Output Template:*  
```
Key Actors: [list]  
Current Challenges: [bulleted list]  
Desired Outcomes: {Outcome 1: [metric+rationale], ...}  
Domain-Specific Terms: {Term: Definition}  
```

**2. Actor/Goal Identification**  
*Input:* Previous output + user role definitions  
*Task:* Map stakeholders to concrete goals using Jobs-To-Be-Done framework  
*Output:*  
```
Actor | Job Statement | Success Criteria  
-------|---------------|-------------------  
Customer | [Verbatim quote] | [Operationalized metric]  
```

**3. Requirement Categorization**  
*Input:* Goals + requirement taxonomy  
*Task:* Classify needs into:  
- Functional (user-facing actions)  
- Non-Functional (performance, security)  
- Business Rules (validation logic)  
*Output Matrix:*  
```
Type | Source Quote | Implied Capability  
-----|--------------|--------------------  
```

**4. Epic Formulation**  
*Input:* Categorized requirements + INVEST criteria  
*Task:* Group related capabilities into epics with clear boundaries  
*Output Structure:*  
```
Epic ID | Covering: [user roles] | Business Value: [impact metric]  
Contains:  
- [Feature 1]  
- [Feature 2]  
Dependencies: [other epics/systems]  
```

**5. Story Decomposition**  
*Input:* Epic + splitting patterns catalog  
*Task:* Break into user stories using SPIDR method (Split by Path, Data, Rules)  
*Validation Check:*  
```python
if not (story.has_actor() and story.has_measurable_outcome()):
    flag_for_review()
```

**6. Acceptance Criteria Generation**  
*Input:* User story + scenario templates  
*Task:* Create testable conditions using Given-When-Then-But format  
*Example Output:*

GIVEN user has unsaved changes

THEN show confirmation modal

```

**7. Dependency Mapping**  
*Input:* All stories + system context diagram  
*Task:* Identify technical/business prerequisites  
*Output Matrix:*  
```
Story ID | Blocks | Blocked By | Parallelizable With  
---------|--------|------------|---------------------

**8. Value Prioritization**  
*Input:* Stories + RICE framework (Reach, Impact, Confidence, Effort)  
*Task:* Score stories relative to business objectives  
*Output:*

Sprint Candidate | RICE Score | Risk Factors

Each step is designed so that its output serves as enriched context for the next prompt, allowing large language models (LLMs) to handle the overall complexity piece by piece.

─────────────────────────────  
Step 1. Preprocess and Segment the Transcript

• Objective: Break the long transcript into manageable segments.  
• What to do:
 – Ask the LLM to scan the transcript and identify natural breaks (e.g., changes in topics, speakers, or technical discussions).  
 – Generate a summary outline that marks sections or “scenes” of the conversation.

• Output Benefit: Provides a roadmap of the discussion so that subsequent analysis isn’t overwhelmed by the transcript’s length.

─────────────────────────────  
Step 2. Extract High-Level Themes and Requirements

• Objective: Identify the main topics, ideas, and potential areas of functionality discussed in the transcript.
• What to do:
 – Use the segmented sections from Step 1 along with any additional context (e.g., known domain details) to prompt the LLM to list high-level themes.
 – This should include functional areas, primary stakeholder concerns, and tentative requirements.
• Example Prompt:  
 "Based on the sections listed below from a Discovery call transcript and our product context [insert brief domain/context description], please list the high-level themes or key areas of functionality discussed. Include indications of potential requirements that may need to be developed."  
• Output Benefit: This step creates a mapping from raw conversation into a set of functional topics, each of which can evolve into an epic or set of user stories.

─────────────────────────────  
Step 3. Drill Down into Specific Functionality per Theme

• Objective: For each theme, extract potential functionalities that can later be converted into discrete user stories.
• What to do:
 – Prompt the LLM to dive deeper into each high-level theme extracted in Step 2.
 – Ask it to detail specific user interactions, system behaviors, or technical capabilities mentioned.
• Example Prompt:

Highlight any potential gaps or areas that may require further clarification from the clients."

Below is one way to achieve movement that “sticks” your character to any surface (cube, sphere, or a custom mesh) by aligning its up vector with the surface normal. The idea is to:

1. Raycast downward (or in the “gravity direction”) to get the hit and its normal.
2. Use the hit.normal to rotate your character so that its “up” aligns with that surface.
3. Project movement input onto the tangent of the surface so that the character moves along it.
4. Optionally apply a custom gravitational force along the surface normal if needed.

Below is an example script in C# using a Rigidbody. (You can also adapt a CharacterController solution if needed.) Attach this script to your character GameObject which should have a Rigidbody component (with “Freeze Rotation” enabled if needed) and a collider (like a CapsuleCollider).

------------------------------------------------------------
using UnityEngine;

public class SurfaceMovement : MonoBehaviour
{
    [Header("Movement Settings")]
    public float moveSpeed = 5f;       // Movement speed along the surface
    public float rotationSpeed = 10f;  // Speed of aligning the character to the surface normal

    [Header("Gravity Settings")]
    public float gravity = 9.81f;      // Strength of gravity to “stick” to the surface
    public float rayDistance = 2f;     // How far down to raycast for the surface

    private Rigidbody rb;

    void Start()
    {
        rb = GetComponent<Rigidbody>();
        // Prevent physics from rotating the character, so we can control it manually.
        rb.freezeRotation = true;
    }

    void FixedUpdate()
    {
        // 1. Raycast from the character’s position in the opposite direction to its current up.
        Ray ray = new Ray(transform.position, -transform.up);
        if (Physics.Raycast(ray, out RaycastHit hit, rayDistance))
        {
            Vector3 surfaceNormal = hit.normal;

            // 2. Align the character’s up vector with the surface normal.
            // Calculate the required rotation to adapt transform.up to the hit normal.
            Quaternion targetRotation = Quaternion.FromToRotation(transform.up, surfaceNormal) * transform.rotation;
            transform.rotation = Quaternion.Slerp(transform.rotation, targetRotation, rotationSpeed * Time.deltaTime);

            // 3. Handle player input and project movement onto the surface.
            float horizontal = Input.GetAxis("Horizontal");
            float vertical = Input.GetAxis("Vertical");

            // Use the input to create a movement vector.
            Vector3 inputVector = new Vector3(horizontal, 0, vertical);
            if (inputVector.sqrMagnitude > 0.001f)
            {
                // Convert input from local character space to world space (you might also use camera forward/right).
                inputVector = transform.TransformDirection(inputVector);
                // Project the input vector onto the tangent plane defined by the hit normal.
                Vector3 moveDirection = Vector3.ProjectOnPlane(inputVector, surfaceNormal).normalized;
                Vector3 movement = moveDirection * moveSpeed;

                // Preserve vertical motion due to gravity (if any) or simply assign velocity on the tangent.
                // Here we add a gravity force along the normal (simulates “sticking” to the surface).
                Vector3 gravityForce = -surfaceNormal * gravity;

                // 4. Apply the combined velocity.
                rb.velocity = movement + gravityForce;
            }
            else
            {
                // When no input, you might still want to “stick” the character to the surface.
                rb.velocity = -surfaceNormal * gravity;
            }
        }
        else
        {
            // No surface detected: fallback to default gravity if necessary.
            rb.AddForce(Physics.gravity, ForceMode.Acceleration);
        }
    }
}

------------------------------------------------------------

How It Works:

• The script fires a ray downward (relative to the character’s current up). You can adjust the ray’s direction if you have a custom gravity system.
• When the ray hits a surface, hit.normal is used to determine the “up” direction for that surface.
• Quaternion.FromToRotation determines the rotation needed to align transform.up with the hit normal. Slerp smoothly interpolates the current rotation to the target.
• The movement input is taken from the Horizontal and Vertical axes and then transformed into world space (or you could use camera-relative movement).
• Vector3.ProjectOnPlane projects that movement onto the surface’s tangent plane, ensuring the character doesn’t move “into” or “away from” the surface.
• Finally, custom gravity (force in the direction opposite to the surface normal) is applied so the character sticks to the surface.

This sample should work in Unity 2023. You can further enhance it by:

• Adding checks for steep slopes.
• Smoothing transitions between surfaces.
• Using a CharacterController or custom physics if needed.

By adapting and expanding on this code, your character can “cling” onto any surface and rotate dynamically as the surface normal changes.
